output.brief: The evidence points away from the Admissions Office and toward the revised merit scholarship schedule. Yield fell from 41.8% to 34.3%, but the fall is concentrated in the two tiers whose awards were cut. Dean's awards went from $14,000 to $9,000 and yield from 45.2% to 31.9%. Merit awards went from $9,000 to $5,000 and yield from 44.9% to 32.3%. Yield was flat in the Presidential tier (awards unchanged) and in the no-award group. Early-action yield fell almost as much as regular-decision yield (7.4 vs 7.5 points), even though early-action decisions went out on time on the old system. So slow regular-decision answers cannot explain most of the drop. Applications and admit quality rose, so a weaker pool is not the cause. The portal delays were real and probably cost some individual students, and I did not test the missing-document claim. I'm fairly confident (about 75–80%). Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take a modelled proposal to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers to the finance committee before award letters go out. Also set a turnaround target for regular decision. Hold the vendor rebuild until document loss is checked.
output.methodChoice: Collected X14 (yield by round) and X10 (yield by scholarship tier) to separate the turnaround, scholarship and general-demand explanations.
